title: Erste Schritte: Sounds, Sie & First Contact
summary: Build the absolute basics of spoken German needed to greet, identify and orient a patient politely.

lessons.title: German Pronunciation for the Clinic: Umlauts, ch and Word Stress

levels.kid:
German has some special sounds that English doesn't have. Learning them helps doctors talk clearly to patients in Germany.

First, the **umlaut**: two little dots on top of a letter, like ä, ö and ü. The dots change the sound. **ü** is tricky: say "ee," then round your lips like you're about to whistle. That's ü, as in **Übelkeit** (feeling sick to your tummy).

Next, **ch**. After "a" or "o" it sounds like a cat hissing softly in the back of your throat, as in **Bauch** (tummy). After "i" or "e" it's a soft sound, like a quiet "hhh," as in **ich** (I).

Last, German words usually get a strong beat at the start: **KOPF**-schmerzen (headache). Clear sounds help patients understand you!
levels.hs:
If you want to work as a doctor in a German-speaking country, clear pronunciation matters. Patients may be old, in pain, or hard of hearing, and a mispronounced word can be misunderstood. Good news: German spelling is fairly **phonetic**, meaning words are mostly said the way they are written.

**Umlauts** are vowels with two dots:
- **ä**: like the "e" in "bed" (Ärztin = female doctor)
- **ö**: say "ay" with rounded lips (hören = to hear)
- **ü**: say "ee" with rounded lips (Übelkeit = nausea)
The dots change meaning: **schon** (already) and **schön** (beautiful) are different words.

**ch** has two main sounds:
- After a, o, u, au: a rough sound in the back of the throat, like Scottish "loch" (Bauch = belly, Knochen = bone)
- After e, i, ä, ö, ü and consonants: a softer, hissing sound (ich = I, Knöchel = ankle, Milch = milk)

Other key sounds: **w** sounds like English "v" (wo = where), **z** sounds like "ts" (Zahn = tooth), and **ei** sounds like English "eye" while **ie** sounds like "ee."

**Word stress**: native German words usually stress the first syllable (**SCHMER**-zen, pain). In compounds, the first part carries the main stress: **KOPF**schmerzen. Example sentence to practise: "Haben Sie Übelkeit oder Bauchschmerzen?" (Do you have nausea or abdominal pain?)
levels.college:
Clinical German depends on a small set of sound contrasts that change meaning or intelligibility. Mastering them early makes later vocabulary much easier.

**Vowels and umlauts.** German vowels are either long and tense or short and lax, and length is often meaningful.
- **ü** /yː/ (long, as in **müde**, tired) vs /ʏ/ (short, as in **Rücken**, back). Tongue as for "ee," lips rounded.
- **ö** /øː/ (**hören**) vs /œ/ (**Knöchel**, ankle)
- **ä** /ɛː/ or /ɛ/ (**Ärztin**, **Gelenk**-like quality)
- Minimal pairs matter: **Bruder/Brüder** (brother/brothers), **schon/schön**.
- Diphthongs: **ei/ai** = "eye" (**Schweiß**, sweat), **eu/äu** = "oy" (**Beule**, lump), **au** = "ow" (**Haut**, skin). Learners often mix **ei** and **ie**: **Bein** (leg) vs **Biene** (bee).

**The ch sounds.**
- **ach-Laut** [x] after a, o, u, au: **Bauch**, **Knochen** (bone). By contrast, **brechen** (to vomit) uses the soft sound because of the preceding e.
- **ich-Laut** [ç] after front vowels, l, n, r: **ich**, **Milch**, **durch**, **Knöchel**.
- Word-initial **ch** varies: **Chirurgie** is usually [ç] in standard German, [k] in much of the south.
- **-ig** at word end is often said like **-ich** in northern standard speech (**schwindlig**, dizzy).

**Consonants.** **Final devoicing** (Auslautverhärtung): b, d, g at the end of a syllable sound like p, t, k (**Kind** "kint"). **z** = /ts/ (**Herz**), **sch** = "sh," **st/sp** at the start of a stem = "sht/shp" (**Stuhl**, stool; **Spritze**, syringe). **r** is usually uvular, and vocalised after vowels (**Ohr**).

**Stress.** Native words stress the stem's first syllable; compounds stress the first element (**BAUCH**schmerzen). Separable prefixes are stressed (**AUS**atmen, breathe out); inseparable ones (be-, ver-, ent-) are not (ver**STOPF**ung, constipation). Latin/Greek loanwords usually stress late: Diagno**se**, Medika**ment**, Neurochirur**gie**.
levels.phd:
From a phonological standpoint, the features that most often impair a non-native clinician's intelligibility in German are vowel quality and length, the dorsal fricative alternation, and stress placement in loanwords.

**Vowel system.** Standard German contrasts tense long and lax short vowels: /iː ɪ yː ʏ uː ʊ eː ɛ øː œ oː ɔ aː a/ plus /ɛː/, which many speakers merge with /eː/. Front rounded vowels /y ø/ are typologically marked and absent from English; anglophone learners typically substitute /u/ or /ʊ/, so **Rücken** (back) drifts toward **rucken** and **Hüfte** (hip) toward an unclear form. Length is signalled orthographically by doubled vowels, vowel + h, and ie (**Sohle**, **Knie**), and shortness by following double consonants (**Mund** vs **Mut** shows the closed-syllable pattern). Unstressed final -e is schwa [ə] and final -er is vocalised [ɐ] (**Fieber** [ˈfiːbɐ], fever).

**Dorsal fricatives.** [ç] and [x] are classically analysed as allophones of a single phoneme: [x] after back vowels, [ç] after front vowels, sonorants, and in the diminutive -chen (**Bäuchlein**, **Mädchen**). The -chen suffix, which yields [ç] even after back vowels (**Kuhchen** vs **Kuchen**), is the textbook argument complicating a pure allophonic account. Regional variation: the -ig suffix is [ɪç] in prescribed standard (Siebs/Duden tradition) but [ɪk] in the south and Austria.

**Obstruents.** Final devoicing neutralises voicing in the syllable coda (**Rad/Rat** homophonous), affecting plural/singular alternations (**Leib/Leiber**). Glottal stops precede vowel-initial morphemes (**be|atmen**, to ventilate), which helps listeners parse compounds; omitting them makes speech sound slurred.

**Prosody.** German is stress-timed. Germanic words take stem-initial stress; compounds follow the compound stress rule (left element prominent: **NIE**renstein, kidney stone). Prefix behaviour is lexically conditioned: separable prefixes are stressed, inseparable unstressed, and a few verbs contrast by stress alone (**UM**fahren vs um**FAH**ren). Greco-Latin vocabulary uses final or penultimate stress by suffix: -ie, -ion, -ös, -al, -ent are stressed (Anäs**the**sie, Infek**tion**, ner**vös**, zere**bral**), while -ik varies (**Kli**nik, but Phy**sik**). Misplacing stress in Fachsprache is a common source of comprehension failure.
levels.expert:
For the practising clinician, pronunciation is a patient-safety and assessment issue, not cosmetics. The Fachsprachprüfung (medical language exam, typically at C1-Medizin level, run by the Landesärztekammern) explicitly rates intelligibility in the patient interview, and examiners respond to errors that force the listener to work.

High-risk confusions at the bedside:
- **Vowel slips**: **müssen** (must) vs **messen** (to measure); **Rücken** vs **Rocken**.
- **ei/ie** reversal in drug and body terms: **Leiste** (groin) vs **Liste**; **Schmerzmittel** stays clear only if the vowels are right.
- **Stress in drug names and Latinisms**: Germans say Ibu**pro**fen, Paraceta**mol**, Hepa**rin**, Amoxi**cil**lin. English-style stress can make a name unrecognisable to nurses during a verbal order, which must still be repeated back (closed-loop communication).
- **Numbers**: fünfzig vs fünfzehn hinge on unstressed -zehn/-zig and the ü; colleagues therefore often say **zwo** for zwei on the phone to avoid confusion with drei.

Register and region: in Bavaria, Austria and Switzerland, patients may use [k] for -ig, a rolled tip r, and Swiss German speakers may keep [x] after front vowels. Understanding dialect matters more than reproducing it; respond in clear Hochdeutsch. Elderly patients and those with presbycusis rely more on consonant contrasts and slower stress-timed rhythm, so lowering pace and keeping the stressed syllable prominent outperforms raising volume.

Useful practice methods: shadowing recorded Anamnese dialogues, minimal-pair drilling with a phonetic transcription (IPA from Duden Aussprachewörterbuch), and recording yourself reading a symptom list (**Kopfschmerzen, Schwindel, Übelkeit, Erbrechen, Sehstörungen**), which for a neurosurgery aspirant doubles as the core red-flag vocabulary for raised intracranial pressure.

Open questions in the field concern how much foreign accent actually affects clinical outcomes; studies of international medical graduates suggest that communication failures arise more from pragmatics and vocabulary than accent, yet patients' perceived trust can drop with heavy accent, which justifies early investment in these sounds.

keyPoints: Umlauts ä, ö, ü change meaning: schon (already) vs schön (beautiful)
ü = say 'ee' with rounded lips, as in Übelkeit (nausea)
ch is rough [x] after a, o, u, au (Bauch) and soft [ç] after front vowels (ich)
Final b, d, g sound like p, t, k (final devoicing)
Native words and compounds stress the first part: KOPFschmerzen
Latin/Greek loanwords and drug names stress late: Diagnose, Infektion

test.q: What do the two dots on ä, ö and ü show?
choices: The vowel has a changed sound
test.explain: Umlaut dots change the vowel sound and can change meaning, as in schon vs schön.

test.q: How do you form the German ü sound?
test.explain: ü uses the tongue position of 'ee' with lips rounded as for 'oo'.

test.q: In which word is ch the rough back-of-throat sound [x]?
test.explain: After a back vowel or au, ch is the ach-Laut [x]. The others follow front vowels or consonants, giving the soft [ç].

test.q: The German letter z is pronounced like:
test.explain: German z = /ts/, as in Herz (heart) and Zahn (tooth).

test.q: Where is the main stress in the compound Kopfschmerzen?
test.explain: German compounds stress the first element: KOPFschmerzen.

test.q: Which word is usually stressed on its final syllable?
test.explain: Loanwords ending in -ion stress the end: Infek-TION. Native words like Fieber stress the first syllable.

test.q: Because of final devoicing, the word Kind ends with a sound like:
test.explain: Syllable-final b, d, g are devoiced to p, t, k, so Kind sounds like 'kint'.

test.q: The German letters ei sound like the English word:
test.explain: ei sounds like 'eye' (Bein), while ie sounds like 'ee' (Knie).

test.q: In the verb ausatmen (to breathe out), which part is stressed?
test.explain: Separable prefixes like aus- carry the stress: AUSatmen. Inseparable prefixes like ver- do not.

test.q: What is the German word for nausea that begins with Ü?
test.explain: Übelkeit means nausea and is a key ü practice word.

test.q: The German word for belly or abdomen, ending in a rough ch sound, is ___.
test.explain: Bauch has the ach-Laut [x] after au.

test.q: German w at the start of a word sounds like which English letter?
test.explain: German w = English v, as in wo (where).

kidTest.q: What are the two little dots on ü called?
kidTest.explain: The dots are called an umlaut and change the sound.

kidTest.q: How do you make the ü sound?
kidTest.explain: Say ee, then round your lips like a whistle.

kidTest.q: What does Bauch mean?
kidTest.explain: Bauch means tummy or belly.

kidTest.q: Where does the strong beat go in Kopfschmerzen?
kidTest.explain: German words usually get the strong beat at the start.

kidTest.q: The German word for 'I' has a soft ch sound. Hint: i _ _
kidTest.explain: ich has the soft, quiet ch sound.

advancedTest.q: Why does Kuhchen (little cow) use [ç] even though ch follows a back vowel?
choices: The diminutive -chen begins a new morpheme with [ç]
Final devoicing turns [x] into [ç] at syllable ends
Southern dialects front this ch sound to [ç] here
The u in Kuh is a fronted vowel in standard speech
advancedTest.explain: The diminutive suffix -chen keeps [ç] across the morpheme boundary, which complicates a purely allophonic analysis of ch.

advancedTest.q: A learner stresses Paracetamol on the second syllable during a verbal order. What is the main clinical risk?
choices: The order is legally invalid in German hospitals
The patient may consider the speech too informal
The nurse may fail to recognise the drug name
The drug will be logged under a new brand name
advancedTest.explain: German speakers stress the final syllable; wrong stress can make a familiar drug name unrecognisable, which is why closed-loop read-back matters.

advancedTest.q: Rad (wheel) and Rat (advice) sound the same in isolation. Which process explains this?
choices: Uvular vocalisation of a final r
advancedTest.explain: Final devoicing neutralises the d/t contrast at the end of a syllable, so both end in [t].

advancedTest.q: Talking with an elderly patient with presbycusis, which strategy is supported in the lesson?
choices: Switch into the patient's regional dialect
Speak much louder at the same quick pace
Slow down and keep stressed syllables clear
Use more Latin terms with late stress
advancedTest.explain: Hearing-impaired listeners rely on consonant contrasts and rhythm, so a slower pace with clear stress helps more than raising volume.

lessons.title: Sie vs. du: Greetings, Introductions and Politeness

levels.kid:
In German, there are two ways to say "you." One is **du**. You use it with friends, family, kids and pets. The other is **Sie**. You use it with grown-ups you don't know well, like a teacher or a patient.

Think of it like wearing clothes. **du** is your comfy pajamas. **Sie** is your nice school outfit. A doctor talking to a grown-up patient always "dresses up" with Sie.

A doctor might say:
- **Guten Tag!** (Good day!)
- **Ich bin Doktor Weber.** (I am Doctor Weber.)
- **Wie heißen Sie?** (What is your name?)

When you leave, you can say **Auf Wiedersehen!** (Goodbye!). Being polite helps patients feel safe and respected.
levels.hs:
German has two words for "you" when speaking to one person: **du** (informal) and **Sie** (formal). Choosing the right one is called the **register**, and in a hospital it matters a lot.

- **du** is for family, friends, children, and often close colleagues.
- **Sie** is for adults you don't know, and it is the standard with adult patients. It is always written with a capital S.

The verb changes with the pronoun:
- **Wie heißt du?** (What's your name?, informal)
- **Wie heißen Sie?** (What's your name?, formal)

The formal Sie uses the same verb form as "they" (sie, plural), which is why it looks like a plural verb.

Useful greetings:
- **Guten Morgen** (good morning), **Guten Tag** (good day), **Guten Abend** (good evening)
- **Hallo** is friendly but casual. In southern Germany and Austria you will hear **Grüß Gott**, and in Switzerland **Grüezi**.

A real example of a doctor introducing herself:

**Guten Tag, Frau Schmidt. Mein Name ist Dr. Weber, ich bin Ihre Ärztin.** (Good day, Mrs. Schmidt. My name is Dr. Weber, I'm your doctor.)

Notice the title: adults are addressed as **Herr** (Mr.) or **Frau** (Mrs./Ms.) plus the surname. Using a first name with an adult patient would feel overly familiar.
levels.college:
**Register in German** is grammatically encoded. Choosing between **du** and **Sie** affects pronouns, verb endings, possessives and imperatives, so it can't be "fixed" by tone of voice alone.

**Formal paradigm (Sie)**, third person plural forms, capitalized:
- Nominative: **Sie** (you). Example: Haben Sie Schmerzen? (Do you have pain?)
- Dative: **Ihnen**. Example: Wie geht es Ihnen? (How are you?)
- Possessive: **Ihr/Ihre**. Example: Ihre Versicherungskarte, bitte. (Your insurance card, please.)

**Informal paradigm (du)**: du / dir / dein. Example: Wie geht es dir? Hast du Schmerzen?

**Clinical rule of thumb**: adult patients get **Sie + Herr/Frau + surname** by default. Common exceptions:
- Children are usually addressed with **du**, roughly until about 14 to 16. With adolescents, asking is respectful: **Darf ich du sagen, oder lieber Sie?**
- Colleagues: many hospital teams, especially nurses and junior doctors, use du among themselves. Senior physicians (Oberarzt, Chefarzt) are addressed with Sie until they offer du.
- The **offer of du** (das Du anbieten) traditionally comes from the older or higher-status person. Don't initiate it with a patient.

**A model introduction (Vorstellung)**:
- Guten Tag, Herr Yilmaz. (greeting + name)
- Mein Name ist Odin, ich bin Medizinstudent. (name + role)
- Ich möchte Ihnen ein paar Fragen stellen. Ist das in Ordnung? (purpose + consent)

**Politeness markers**: **bitte** (please), **danke** (thanks), **Entschuldigung** (excuse me), and the softening subjunctive **könnten Sie...?** (could you...?) or **ich würde gern...** (I would like to...). Leave-taking: **Auf Wiedersehen**, or **Gute Besserung!** (Get well soon!).
levels.phd:
German **T/V distinction** (from Latin tu/vos) is the classic case analyzed by Brown and Gilman (1960) in "The Pronouns of Power and Solidarity." They described a historical shift from a **power semantic**, where asymmetric use signaled hierarchy (superior says du, inferior answers Sie), toward a **solidarity semantic**, where reciprocal du signals intimacy or group membership and reciprocal Sie signals distance or respect. In modern clinical German, reciprocal Sie is the norm with adult patients. Asymmetric address, where the doctor uses du while the patient must use Sie, is generally perceived as condescending, especially toward elderly or cognitively impaired patients.

**Morphosyntax of Sie.** The formal pronoun derives from the third-person plural. It takes plural agreement even when addressing one person: Sie sind, Sie haben. Its forms are Sie/Ihnen/Ihr, distinguished in writing from sie (she/they) only by capitalization. In speech this creates ambiguity: "Haben sie Fieber?" could mean "Do they have a fever?" Context resolves it.

**Imperatives.** The formal imperative inverts verb and pronoun: **Setzen Sie sich, bitte** (Please sit down). The du imperative drops the pronoun: Setz dich. Exam commands are covered later, but the formal pattern starts with first contact.

**Mitigation.** Brown and Levinson's politeness theory treats requests as **face-threatening acts**. German speakers soften them with the **Konjunktiv II** (könnten, würden, hätten), modal particles (**mal**, **doch**, **bitte**) and asking permission. "Könnten Sie mir bitte kurz Ihren Namen sagen?" is far softer than "Name?"

**Sociolinguistic variation.** Du has spread since the 1968 student movement, and further through workplaces, IKEA-style marketing and online speech. Use differs by region and age, and Austria and Switzerland add their own greeting forms (Grüß Gott, Servus, Grüezi). Address terms also carry titles. **Herr Doktor / Frau Doktor** is still common from patients, and Austria in particular preserves academic titles in address.
levels.expert:
Practical pitfalls for a non-native clinician in German-speaking hospitals:

- **Switching mid-conversation.** Learners often start with Sie, then slip into dir/dein forms ("Wie geht es dir?") through habit. Patients notice this immediately. Drill the whole set together: Sie / Ihnen / Ihr.
- **Elderly and dementia care.** Using du or first names with elderly residents ("Oma," "Schätzchen") is criticized in German care ethics as infantilizing (*Elderspeak*). Keep Sie unless the patient explicitly asks otherwise, and document that preference.
- **Children and adolescents.** Pediatric staff use du with children. With teenagers, an explicit question works well: "Ist es okay, wenn ich du sage?" Parents are still addressed with Sie.
- **Team culture.** Many German clinics now use du across the team, sometimes even with the Chefarzt. Others remain hierarchical. Watch first and mirror. Accepting an offered du ("Ich bin der Thomas") is normal; refusing it can seem cold.
- **Name plus role at every contact.** British-born campaigns like "Hello, my name is" have equivalents in German patient-safety culture. A full Vorstellung (name, role, purpose) reduces identification errors and builds trust. It is also tested in the communication part of the **Fachsprachprüfung (FSP)**.

High-yield clinical phrases:
- **Darf ich mich kurz vorstellen?** (May I briefly introduce myself?)
- **Ich bin heute für Sie zuständig.** (I'm responsible for you today.)
- **Wie darf ich Sie ansprechen?** (How may I address you?) This is valuable with nonbinary patients or uncertain names.
- **Haben Sie noch Fragen?** (Do you have any more questions?)
- **Ich wünsche Ihnen gute Besserung.** (I wish you a speedy recovery.)

**Grammar note.** Watch case after formal verbs. Use **helfen + Dativ** in "Kann ich Ihnen helfen?" but **fragen + Akkusativ** in "Darf ich Sie etwas fragen?" Mixing Ihnen and Sie here is a classic FSP error.

**Open question.** Gender-inclusive address beyond Herr/Frau is evolving. Many hospitals now use "Guten Tag, [first name + surname]" in letters and allow neutral address on request.

keyPoints: du is informal; Sie is formal and is the default with adult patients
Sie is capitalized and uses third-person plural verb forms
Formal forms come as a set: Sie, Ihnen, Ihr
Address adults as Herr/Frau + surname
Introduce yourself with name, role and purpose
Soften requests with bitte and könnten/würden

test.q: Which form of 'you' should a doctor use with an adult patient by default?
test.explain: Sie is the formal 'you' and is the standard with adult patients. du is informal.

test.q: How do you formally ask 'How are you?' in German?
test.explain: Ihnen is the formal dative. 'Wie geht es dir?' is informal, and the heißen questions ask for a name.

test.q: The formal Sie uses the same verb form as which pronoun?
test.explain: Formal Sie comes from the third-person plural, so it takes plural verb forms like 'Sie sind'.

test.q: How should you address an adult patient named Anna Schmidt?
test.explain: Adults are addressed as Herr or Frau plus surname. A first name feels overly familiar.

test.q: Which greeting is typical in southern Germany and Austria?
test.explain: Grüß Gott is typical in Bavaria and Austria. Grüezi is Swiss.

test.q: Who traditionally offers the switch to du?
test.explain: The offer of du traditionally comes from the older or higher-status person.

test.q: Which phrase politely softens a request to an adult patient?
choices: Name? Schnell, ich habe keine Zeit.
Sag mir bitte schnell deinen Namen.
Geben Sie mir jetzt sofort Ihren Namen.
Könnten Sie bitte Ihren Namen sagen?
test.explain: Konjunktiv II (könnten) plus bitte and the formal Sie softens the request. The du version is too informal for an adult patient, and the others are curt commands.

test.q: What does 'Gute Besserung!' mean?
test.explain: Gute Besserung wishes a patient a speedy recovery.

test.q: With which person is du usually appropriate in a clinic?
test.explain: Children are usually addressed with du. Unfamiliar adults and senior physicians get Sie.

test.q: The formal possessive 'your', as in '___ Versicherungskarte, bitte', is capitalized just like Sie.
test.explain: Ihr/Ihre is the formal possessive, capitalized like Sie.

test.q: What is the formal dative form of 'you' (as in 'Kann ich ___ helfen?')?
test.explain: helfen takes the dative, so the formal form is Ihnen.

test.q: The German word for 'please' is ___.
test.explain: bitte is the basic politeness marker in requests.

kidTest.q: Which 'you' do you use with a friend?
kidTest.explain: du is the friendly, informal 'you'.

kidTest.q: Which 'you' does a doctor use with a grown-up patient?
kidTest.explain: Sie is the polite 'you' for grown-ups you don't know well.

kidTest.q: What does 'Guten Tag' mean?
kidTest.explain: Guten Tag is a polite hello: good day.

kidTest.q: What does 'Auf Wiedersehen' mean?
kidTest.explain: Auf Wiedersehen is a polite goodbye.

kidTest.q: Fill in the polite word for 'you' that starts with S: S _ _
kidTest.explain: Sie is the polite 'you' a doctor uses with grown-ups.

advancedTest.q: In Brown and Gilman's terms, a doctor saying du to an elderly patient who must reply with Sie reflects:
choices: A purely regional greeting pattern in Austria
The solidarity semantic shown by reciprocal du
The distance semantic shown by reciprocal Sie
The power semantic shown by asymmetric address
advancedTest.explain: Asymmetric address encodes hierarchy, which is Brown and Gilman's power semantic, and patients perceive it as condescending.

advancedTest.q: Why is 'Haben sie Fieber?' potentially ambiguous when spoken?
choices: The verb haben has no plural form in German
Formal Sie and plural sie sound identical
Fieber is a noun that changes gender by region
Spoken German drops pronouns in questions
advancedTest.explain: Sie (you) and sie (they) differ only in capitalization in writing, so in speech only context tells them apart.

advancedTest.q: A learner says 'Darf ich Ihnen etwas fragen?' What is the error?
choices: fragen takes dative, so dir is needed
darf is informal and should be dürfen
fragen takes accusative, so Sie is needed
etwas should come before the pronoun
advancedTest.explain: fragen governs the accusative, so the formal pronoun is Sie. Ihnen is dative, used with verbs like helfen.

advancedTest.q: A clinician unsure how a nonbinary patient wishes to be addressed should most appropriately:
choices: Ask 'Wie darf ich Sie ansprechen?' and record it
Use the first name without asking first
Use Herr Doktor as a neutral title
Use du to avoid choosing Herr or Frau
advancedTest.explain: Asking keeps the formal Sie while respecting the patient's preference. Switching to du or first names trades respect for convenience.

lessons.title: Spelling Names with the German Spelling Alphabet (Buchstabiertafel)

levels.kid:
Have you ever said your name and someone wrote it wrong? On the phone, letters like **M** and **N**, or **B** and **D**, sound almost the same.

So German speakers use a **Buchstabiertafel**, a spelling chart. Each letter gets a word that starts with it. Today the official words are German cities:
- **A wie Aachen**
- **B wie Berlin**
- **M wie München**
- **N wie Nürnberg**

"Wie" means "like" or "as in." So you say "M wie München" to show you mean M, not N.

In a hospital this matters a lot. If a name is spelled wrong, the doctor might find the wrong patient's papers. A clear spelling chart keeps patients safe.
levels.hs:
When you meet a patient, you need to write their name exactly right. To ask, you say: **"Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?"** (Could you spell that, please?). The verb **buchstabieren** means "to spell."

Germans spell aloud using the **Buchstabiertafel** (spelling table), set by the national standard **DIN 5009**. Each letter is linked to a code word, said as "letter **wie** word":
- A wie Aachen, B wie Berlin, C wie Chemnitz, D wie Düsseldorf
- K wie Köln, L wie Leipzig, M wie München, S wie Salzwedel, Z wie Zwickau

Since **2022**, the official code words are city names. Before that, Germany used first names like **Anton, Berta, Cäsar, Dora**, and many older people still use them. Both are understood.

German has extra letters too:
- **Ä, Ö, Ü** are said as "Umlaut A" and so on (for example "Ü wie Umlaut Unna")
- **ß** is called **Eszett** ("scharfes S")

Some letters are named differently from English: J is **"Jott,"** V is **"Fau,"** W is **"We,"** Z is **"Zett."**

Real example: the surname Meier can also be written Maier, Mayer or Meyer. All four sound the same. A nurse might ask, "Mit ei oder ai?" (With ei or ai?). One wrong letter can attach a lab result to the wrong person.
levels.college:
Spelling a name aloud is a core patient-safety skill. German has many **homophonous surnames**: Meier/Maier/Mayer/Meyer, Schmidt/Schmitt/Schmid, Hoffmann/Hofmann, Fischer/Vischer. Phone lines and noisy wards blur similar consonants (M/N, B/D/P/T, F/S).

**The standard.** DIN 5009 defines the German spelling table. The **2022 revision** (DIN 5009:2022-06) replaced personal names with cities:
- A Aachen, B Berlin, C Chemnitz, D Düsseldorf, E Essen, F Frankfurt, G Goslar, H Hamburg, I Ingelheim, J Jena, K Köln, L Leipzig, M München
- N Nürnberg, O Offenbach, P Potsdam, Q Quickborn, R Rostock, S Salzwedel, T Tübingen, U Unna, V Völklingen, W Wuppertal, X Xanten, Y Ypsilon, Z Zwickau
- Ä Umlaut Aachen, Ö Umlaut Offenbach, Ü Umlaut Unna, ß Eszett

The traditional names remain widespread: Anton, Berta, Cäsar, Dora, Emil, Friedrich, Gustav, Heinrich, Ida, Julius, Kaufmann, Ludwig, Martha, Nordpol, Otto, Paula, Quelle, Richard, Samuel/Siegfried, Theodor, Ulrich, Viktor, Wilhelm, Xanthippe, Ypsilon, Zacharias/Zeppelin, plus Ärger, Ökonom, Übermut.

**Useful phrases:**
- **Wie schreibt man Ihren Nachnamen?** (How is your surname written?)
- **Mit Doppel-s oder mit Eszett?** (With double s or ß?)
- **Groß oder klein?** (Capital or lowercase?) for name particles such as "von"
- **Mit Bindestrich?** (With a hyphen?)
- **Ich wiederhole:** M wie München, E wie Essen... (I'll repeat.)

**Grammar note:** "wie" here is a comparison particle, not the question word "how." It does not change the case of the noun after it. Buchstabieren is a regular verb: ich buchstabiere, Sie buchstabieren.

Always **read back** what you wrote. This closed-loop step catches errors that a single hearing misses.
levels.phd:
The structure of a spelling alphabet is a problem in **acoustic discriminability**. A good code word is long enough to survive degraded transmission, has a distinctive stressed syllable, and does not resemble other code words. Single letter names cluster badly: German /be:/, /de:/, /te:/, /pe:/, /tse:/ (C), and /e:/ differ only in an onset consonant that band-limited telephone audio (historically ~300–3400 Hz) partly removes.

**History.** The first German spelling tables (around 1890) used numbers, later replaced by first names. In **1934** the Nazi regime removed names regarded as Jewish: David became Dora, Jacob became Jot, Nathan became Nordpol, Samuel became Siegfried, and Zacharias became Zeppelin. Postwar versions only partly reversed this. Samuel and Zacharias returned in some versions, but Dora and Nordpol stayed, and Siegfried and Zeppelin remained common in practice. Prompted largely by Michael Blume, Baden-Württemberg's commissioner against antisemitism, the DIN committee published a new table in **2022** built on city names. The pre-1934 Weimar-era name list was published as an appendix for remembrance.

**Design choices in 2022.** Cities avoid gender and ethnic imbalance in name lists and give regional coverage. Some choices are deliberately unusual for discriminability or initial-letter reasons (Quickborn, Salzwedel, Ingelheim). Y kept **Ypsilon**, because few German places begin with Y. Umlauts are coded as "Umlaut + base word" instead of separate words, which shows they are modifications of base letters.

**Orthographic nuance.** Umlaut transliteration (ü → ue) is common in IT systems and passports, so Müller may appear as MUELLER. ß has no capital in traditional use, but **capital ẞ** has been officially allowed since 2017. In uppercase forms, ß is often written SS, which creates false mismatches during record matching. Names with "sch" were coded as Sch wie Schule in the old table. In the 2022 version they are spelled letter by letter.
levels.expert:
In clinical German, spelling interacts with **patient identification**, where errors cause wrong-patient orders, mislabeled specimens and duplicate records. Hospital information systems (KIS) match on surname, first name and birthdate. Each orthographic variant (Müller/Mueller, Strauß/Strauss, ö/oe) can create a duplicate chart or hide an existing one. When a search fails, try umlaut and ß variants before creating a new record.

**Regional variation.** Austria (ÖNORM A 1081) uses its own name table, for example K wie Konrad, X wie Xaver, Z wie Zürich. Switzerland has another. Many German staff mix old and new tables, and that is fine. The rule is consistency within one spelling and confirmation at the end. Avoid inventing code words on the spot, because ad hoc words ("M wie Mama") are less discriminable.

**International names.** Many patients have names transliterated from Arabic, Turkish, Cyrillic or other scripts, and one person may appear in several forms (Mohammed/Muhammad/Mehmet). Ask the patient to spell exactly as written on the **Versichertenkarte** or ID, rather than guessing from the sound. Diacritics need explicit words: **"E mit Akut"** (é), **"S mit Hatschek"** (š), **"C mit Cedille"** (ç). Turkish ı (dotless i) and ğ often get lost in German systems, so record the official form.

**Communication technique.** In emergencies and on the phone with the Rettungsleitstelle, laboratory or another hospital, use closed loop: the receiver reads back **"Ich wiederhole..."** and the sender confirms with **"Richtig"** or corrects. For critical lab values phoned through, the read-back should include the spelled name. Mark **Nachname** versus **Vorname** explicitly, because order varies across cultures. Ask about **Geburtsname** (shown as "geb.") when matching older records.

**ICAO alphabet.** The international alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) appears in aviation, military and some air-rescue (Luftrettung) settings, but on a German ward the DIN table is expected.

**Exam relevance.** In the Fachsprachprüfung, examiners often play patients with tricky surnames. Asking smoothly "Könnten Sie mir Ihren Nachnamen bitte buchstabieren?" and reading it back shows safety awareness as well as fluency.

keyPoints: Buchstabieren = to spell; ask 'Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?'
DIN 5009 defines the German spelling table: say 'letter wie word'
Since 2022 code words are cities (A wie Aachen); old names (Anton, Berta) are still common
Ä/Ö/Ü are spelled as 'Umlaut A/O/U'; ß is called Eszett
Letter names differ: J = Jott, V = Fau, W = We, Z = Zett
Read back spellings: one wrong letter can mean the wrong patient record

test.q: What does 'Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?' mean?
choices: Could you write that down, please?
test.explain: Buchstabieren means to spell aloud letter by letter.

test.q: Which German standard defines the official spelling table?
test.explain: DIN 5009 is the German standard for spelling aloud. DIN A4 is a paper size, not a spelling standard.

test.q: Since the 2022 revision, what are the official code words based on?
test.explain: DIN 5009:2022 replaced personal names with cities, such as A wie Aachen and B wie Berlin.

test.q: How is Ü spelled in the 2022 table?
test.explain: In the 2022 table, umlauts are coded as 'Umlaut' plus the base word for the plain letter, and U is Unna. Ulrich is the U word from the traditional table. Übermut is the traditional word for Ü. Überlingen does not appear in the table.

test.q: What is the German name of the letter W?
test.explain: W is called 'We' in German. 'Fau' is the name of V.

test.q: In the traditional name-based table, A was spelled as:
test.explain: The traditional German table began Anton, Berta, Cäsar. Aachen is the 2022 city word, and Alfa is ICAO.

test.q: Why might a nurse ask 'Mit ei oder ai?' about the name Meier?
choices: Ei and ai mark different genders
Meier is usually written with ä
test.explain: Meier, Maier, Mayer and Meyer are homophones, so the spelling has to be confirmed.

test.q: After writing down a spelled name, what is the safest next step?
choices: Search the chart by first name
Ask the patient to write it later
Spell it using the ICAO alphabet
test.explain: Reading back (closed loop) catches errors that one hearing misses.

test.q: In 'M wie München,' the word 'wie' functions as:
test.explain: Here wie means 'like/as in' and does not change the case of the noun after it.

test.q: What is the German name for the letter ß?
test.explain: ß is called Eszett or scharfes S.

test.q: The German letter J is pronounced ___.
test.explain: J is 'Jott' in German, not 'jay' as in English.

test.q: What German verb means 'to spell (aloud)'?
test.explain: Buchstabieren comes from Buchstabe (letter).

kidTest.q: What is a Buchstabiertafel?
choices: A chart that helps spell letters
A list of medicines for doctors
A table where patients eat lunch
kidTest.explain: It gives each letter a word so letters are not mixed up.

kidTest.q: What does 'wie' mean in 'M wie München'?
kidTest.explain: M wie München means M, like in München.

kidTest.q: Why use special words on the phone?
choices: Phones work badly with long words
kidTest.explain: M and N, or B and D, sound similar on the phone.

kidTest.q: Why must a hospital spell names right?
choices: So the doctor can write faster
So it finds the right papers
kidTest.explain: A wrong letter could bring up the wrong patient's papers.

kidTest.q: B wie ... ? It's Germany's capital city: B _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: B wie Berlin is in the official German spelling chart.

advancedTest.q: A patient search for 'Müller' finds nothing, but the patient says she was treated there before. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: Her record was deleted after the 2022 DIN change
The system searches patients by first name
Her surname was coded using Austrian code words
Her record was stored under an umlaut-free variant
advancedTest.explain: IT systems often transliterate ü as ue (MUELLER), which creates hidden or duplicate records. Spelling tables do not affect how records are stored.

advancedTest.q: Why do spelling tables use multisyllable code words instead of letter names alone?
choices: Code words encode where each letter sits in the alphabet
Single letter names are harder to write down
Telephone bandwidth blurs the consonants that separate letter names
German letter names are mostly vowels
advancedTest.explain: Letter names like Be, De, Te and Pe differ only in an onset consonant. Band-limited audio degrades that consonant, while longer words keep distinctive cues.

advancedTest.q: Which statement best reflects the history behind the 2022 DIN 5009 revision?
choices: Some 1934 replacements such as Nordpol persisted until 2022
The revision was triggered by Austrian standardization
City names were adopted to match the ICAO alphabet
Postwar versions fully reversed the 1934 name removals
advancedTest.explain: Postwar restoration was partial. Words like Dora and Nordpol remained until the city-based table replaced the name list.

advancedTest.q: A colleague spells over the phone using a mix of old names and new city words. What is the best response?
choices: Accept it and read the spelling back
Ask to repeat the spelling in ICAO words
Ask them to switch to city words instead
Write the name based on how it sounds
advancedTest.explain: Both tables are understood. Safety comes from consistency within one spelling and closed-loop confirmation.

lessons.title: Numbers, Dates, Times and Birthdates (Geburtsdatum)

levels.kid:
Doctors in Germany need numbers all day. How old are you? When is your birthday? What time is it?

German numbers have a funny trick. For 21, Germans say **einundzwanzig**. That means "one-and-twenty." The small number comes first, like reading a clock backwards!

Birthdays are written with the day first: 03.05. means the 3rd of May, not March 5th.

Time has a trick too. **Halb drei** means "half three," but it is really 2:30. It is halfway TO three o'clock.

Why does the doctor ask your birthday? Lots of people share the same name. Your name plus your birthday helps make sure the right medicine goes to the right person.
levels.hs:
Numbers are a safety tool in the clinic. Here are the basics:

- **Cardinal numbers**: eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 21 up, the unit comes before the ten: **einundzwanzig** (21), **siebenundvierzig** (47). Mixing these up is a classic error: 47 can become 74.
- **Zwo** is often said instead of zwei on the phone or in loud wards, because zwei and drei sound alike.
- **Dates** use day.month.year: 03.05.1975 is 3 May 1975. Dates are spoken with ordinal numbers: "am **dritten** Mai."
- **Years** are said in hundreds: 1975 = **neunzehnhundertfünfundsiebzig**. From 2000: **zweitausendacht** (2008).
- **Time**: hospitals use the 24-hour clock: "um vierzehn Uhr" (2 p.m.). In everyday speech, **halb drei** means 2:30, not 3:30.

Key phrases:
- **Wann sind Sie geboren?** (When were you born?)
- **Ich bin am dritten Mai 1975 geboren.** (I was born on 3 May 1975.)
- **Wie alt sind Sie?** (How old are you?)

Example: before giving a medication, a nurse asks "Wie ist Ihr Name und Ihr Geburtsdatum?" Name plus **Geburtsdatum** (date of birth) are two separate identifiers. Using both prevents mix-ups between patients with the same name.
levels.college:
**Number building.** German compounds numbers into a single written word, unit before ten: 365 = dreihundertfünfundsechzig. Watch the spelling changes: **sechzehn** and **sechzig** (not sechszehn), **siebzehn** and **siebzig** (not siebenzehn), and **dreißig** with ß. Eins becomes **ein** before -und: einundzwanzig.

**Ordinals for dates.** Add **-te** for 1-19 and **-ste** from 20 up, with irregular forms:
- erste, zweite, **dritte**, vierte, ... **siebte**, **achte**
- zwanzigste, einunddreißigste

After "am" (dative), the ending is -en: **am ersten Januar**, **am zwanzigsten Juli**. Written, the ordinal takes a period: am 1. Januar. To ask the date: **Der Wievielte ist heute?** or **Welches Datum haben wir heute?**

**Months**: Januar, Februar, März, April, Mai, **Juni**, **Juli**, August, September, Oktober, November, Dezember. Juni and Juli are easily confused, so speakers say **Juno** and **Julei** for clarity. In Austria, January is **Jänner**.

**Clock time.**
- Formal / clinical: **14:30 Uhr** = vierzehn Uhr dreißig.
- Colloquial: **Viertel nach zwei** (2:15), **halb drei** (2:30), **Viertel vor drei** (2:45).

**Clinical numbers.**
- German uses a **decimal comma**: 37,5 °C = siebenunddreißig Komma fünf Grad.
- Blood pressure 120/80 = **hundertzwanzig zu achtzig**.
- Phone numbers are often read in pairs: 47 11 = siebenundvierzig elf.

**Taking the birthdate.** Ask "Wann sind Sie geboren?" or "Ihr Geburtsdatum, bitte?" Repeat it back in digits: "Also, der dritte Mai neunzehnhundertfünfundsiebzig, richtig?" This read-back closes the loop and catches errors.
levels.phd:
Several features of the German number system are linguistically marked and predict specific clinical errors.

**Inversion (Zahlendreher).** German shares unit-before-ten order with Dutch and older English ("four-and-twenty"). Speech order (7-und-40) runs opposite to written digit order (4-7), so listeners transcribing a number must hold the unit in working memory before writing the ten first. Psycholinguistic studies of German-speaking children, notably work on transcoding by Zuber, Pixner, Moeller and Nuerk, show more inversion errors than in languages with consistent order. The term **Zahlendreher** (number twister) names this everyday slip. In the clinic it can swap a room, a lab value or a birth year.

**Grammar of dates.** Ordinals inflect like adjectives. "Heute ist **der** dritte Mai" (nominative, -e) contrasts with "**am** dritten Mai" (am = an dem, dative, -en) and the letter heading "Berlin, **den** 3. Mai" (accusative, -en). The period after a numeral marks it as ordinal in writing; omitting it changes the meaning.

**Regional time expressions.** Besides "Viertel nach drei" (3:15), speakers in parts of eastern and southern Germany and Austria say **viertel vier** (a quarter of the way to four, so 3:15) and **dreiviertel vier** (3:45). Both systems count toward the coming hour, as halb does. A northern-trained doctor may hear "viertel vier" as 3:45 or 4:15. Clinicians therefore restate times in 24-hour digits.

**Disambiguation conventions.** Spoken **zwo** (for zwei) and **Juno / Julei** are informal versions of the radio-procedure principle seen in the spelling alphabet: make sound-alike items acoustically distinct.

**Date formats.** DIN 5008 lists day.month.year (03.05.1975) alongside ISO 8601 year-month-day (1975-05-03) for formal writing. Imported records from US systems (month/day) create ambiguity for any day 12 or below.
levels.expert:
**Identification as patient safety.** German hospitals follow the internationally recommended standard of at least two identifiers, typically full name and **Geburtsdatum**, before medication, transfusion, imaging or surgery. The Aktionsbündnis Patientensicherheit recommends **active** identification: the patient states the data, rather than answering yes to "Sie sind Herr Müller, geboren am 3. Mai?" Confused, sedated or anxious patients will often agree to anything. Correct phrasing:
- **Nennen Sie mir bitte Ihren vollständigen Namen und Ihr Geburtsdatum.**
- Then compare against the wristband (**Patientenarmband**) and chart.

**Read-back in handover and on the phone.** For critical values, the receiver repeats in digits and spells the inversion out: "Kalium sechs Komma acht, also sechs, Komma, acht." Some clinicians read multi-digit numbers digit by digit ("vier, sieben") to avoid the Zahlendreher entirely.

**Pitfalls for non-native doctors**, frequently noted in Fachsprachprüfung feedback:
- Saying "halb drei" and meaning 3:30 (English "half three" means 3:30 in British usage, the opposite of German).
- Dropping the ordinal ending: "am drei Mai" instead of **am dritten Mai**.
- Using a decimal point aloud; German says **Komma**, and a written point can be read as a thousands separator (1.500 = fifteen hundred).
- Confusing **fünfzehn** (15) and **fünfzig** (50) at the bedside, a classic mishearing for older or hard-of-hearing patients.

**Orientation testing.** Dates double as a neurological screen. Asking **"Welches Datum haben wir heute?"** and **"Welcher Wochentag ist heute?"** checks temporal orientation (zeitlich orientiert), one domain of "zu allen Qualitäten orientiert" (oriented to time, place, person and situation). In a neurosurgical ward after a craniotomy, a new failure here can be an early sign of deterioration. Note the answer exactly; "Mai 1975" when asked today's date is clinically meaningful.

**Age phrasing.** Notes use "**68-jähriger Patient**" (68-year-old male) or "Patientin, 72 Jahre"; the hyphenated adjective form is standard in the Arztbrief.

keyPoints: German numbers put the unit before the ten: 47 = siebenundvierzig
Zwo replaces zwei to avoid confusion with drei
Dates run day.month.year and use ordinals: am dritten Mai
Halb drei means 2:30; hospitals use the 24-hour clock
German uses a decimal comma: 37,5 = siebenunddreißig Komma fünf
Name plus Geburtsdatum, stated by the patient, identifies them safely

test.q: How do you say 21 in German?
test.explain: German puts the unit first, joined by und, and eins shortens to ein: einundzwanzig.

test.q: A patient says her appointment is at halb drei. What time is that?
test.explain: Halb drei means halfway to three, so 2:30. Reading it as 3:30 is the classic English-speaker error.

test.q: A German chart lists a birthdate of 03.05.1975. What date is this?
test.explain: German dates go day.month.year, so 03.05.1975 is the 3rd of May 1975.

test.q: Why do German speakers often say zwo instead of zwei on the phone?
choices: It is the written legal form
test.explain: Zwei and drei sound alike over a bad line, so zwo makes the number acoustically distinct.

test.q: Which question asks a patient for their date of birth?
test.explain: Wann sind Sie geboren? means When were you born? Wie alt sind Sie? asks only for age.

test.q: How is a temperature of 37,5 °C read aloud?
test.explain: German uses a decimal comma, spoken as Komma, with the normal unit-first number.

test.q: Fill in: Ich bin am ___ Juli geboren (the 20th).
test.explain: From 20 up, ordinals use -ste; after am the ending is -en, giving zwanzigsten.

test.q: How is the year 1975 normally said?
test.explain: Years before 2000 are said in hundreds: neunzehnhundert plus fünfundsiebzig.

test.q: Why does a nurse ask for the birthdate as well as the name?
test.explain: Many patients share names; name plus date of birth gives two independent identifiers and prevents mix-ups.

test.q: In colloquial German, 2:45 is Viertel ___ drei.
test.explain: Viertel vor drei means a quarter before three, 2:45. Viertel nach zwei is 2:15.

test.q: Which clarity form do speakers use for Juli so it is not confused with Juni?
test.explain: Julei (and Juno for Juni) make the two months easy to tell apart when spoken.

test.q: How is blood pressure 120/80 read aloud in German?
test.explain: The slash is spoken as zu: hundertzwanzig zu achtzig.

kidTest.q: How do Germans say 21?
kidTest.explain: They say one-and-twenty: einundzwanzig.

kidTest.q: What time is halb drei?
kidTest.explain: It means halfway to three, so 2:30.

kidTest.q: In a German date, what comes first?
kidTest.explain: Germans write the day first, then month, then year.

kidTest.q: Why does the doctor ask your birthday?
choices: To make sure it is you
kidTest.explain: Name plus birthday helps the right medicine reach the right person.

kidTest.q: In German, the number 3 is d _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Drei means three.

advancedTest.q: A doctor trained in Hamburg hears a nurse in Dresden say a scan is at viertel vier. What is the safest response?
choices: Ask the nurse to switch to using halb instead
Assume it means 3:45 because vier is the hour named
Assume it means 4:15 since viertel counts past the hour
Restate the time as 15:15 Uhr in digits and confirm
advancedTest.explain: In eastern and southern usage viertel vier means 3:15, which a northerner may misread. Restating in 24-hour digits removes the ambiguity.

advancedTest.q: Why is asking 'Sie sind Herr Müller, geboren am 3. Mai?' weaker than asking the patient to state their data?
choices: It omits the year, which is the key identifier
It uses the wrong ordinal ending for the date
It addresses the patient with an informal form
A confused patient may simply agree with it
advancedTest.explain: Closed confirmation questions invite a yes from sedated or anxious patients. Active identification makes the patient produce the data.

advancedTest.q: Why are Zahlendreher errors more common when transcribing spoken German numbers than English ones?
choices: Spoken order puts the unit first, opposite to writing
German uses a decimal comma instead of a point
German has unique single words for numbers up to 99
German digits are written right to left on charts
advancedTest.explain: Siebenundvierzig is spoken 7 then 40 but written 4 then 7, so the listener must reorder, which invites inversion slips.

advancedTest.q: Two days after a craniotomy, a patient asked 'Welches Datum haben wir heute?' answers 'Mai 1975'. What is the best interpretation?
choices: A normal effect of the 24-hour clock in hospital
A pronunciation slip that needs no documentation
Possible new temporal disorientation worth reporting
Evidence the patient misheard Datum as Geburtsdatum
advancedTest.explain: Date questions test temporal orientation; a new failure after neurosurgery can signal deterioration and should be documented exactly and escalated.

lessons.title: Taking Personal Data: Name, Address, Insurance (Krankenkasse)

levels.kid:
When you visit a new doctor in Germany, the first thing someone does is fill in a form about you. It is like making a name tag that the hospital keeps.

They ask:
- **Wie heißen Sie?** (What is your name?)
- **Wo wohnen Sie?** (Where do you live?)
- **Bei welcher Krankenkasse sind Sie?** (Which health insurance do you have?)

A **Krankenkasse** is like a big shared piggy bank. Lots of people put money in every month. When someone gets sick, the piggy bank helps pay the doctor.

Most people show a small plastic card called the **Gesundheitskarte** (health card). The doctor's computer reads it, a bit like a library card. It helps make sure the right person gets the right care.
levels.hs:
Before any history or exam, the reception staff or doctor records the patient's **Personalien** (personal data). In German you stay polite with **Sie**, and you address people as **Herr** or **Frau** plus the surname.

Key questions and words:
- **Wie ist Ihr Name?** or **Wie heißen Sie?** (What is your name?)
- **Vorname** (first name), **Nachname** or **Familienname** (surname)
- **Wie ist Ihre Adresse?** (What is your address?) The answer includes **Straße** (street), **Hausnummer** (house number), **Postleitzahl** (postcode, five digits in Germany) and **Wohnort** (town).
- **Bei welcher Krankenkasse sind Sie versichert?** (Which health insurance fund are you insured with?)
- **Haben Sie Ihre Versichertenkarte dabei?** (Do you have your insurance card with you?)
- **Wer ist Ihr Hausarzt?** (Who is your family doctor?)
- **Wen sollen wir im Notfall benachrichtigen?** (Whom should we contact in an emergency?)

Germany has two insurance systems. About 90% of people are **gesetzlich versichert** (statutorily insured) through a **Krankenkasse** such as the AOK, Techniker Krankenkasse (TK), Barmer or DAK. About 10% are **privat versichert** (privately insured).

Example at reception:
"Guten Tag, Frau Weber. Bei welcher Krankenkasse sind Sie versichert?" "Bei der AOK." "Danke. Dann brauche ich bitte Ihre Karte."
levels.college:
Recording **Personalien** is the first clinical speech act in a German practice or ward. It is formulaic, so learning it as fixed phrases pays off quickly.

**Identity**
- **Wie heißen Sie mit Vor- und Nachnamen?** (Your first and last name?)
- **Geburtsname** (birth name, often asked for married patients)
- **Familienstand**: **ledig** (single), **verheiratet** (married), **geschieden** (divorced), **verwitwet** (widowed)
- **Staatsangehörigkeit** (nationality), **Beruf** (occupation, which is clinically relevant for exposures)
- **Personalausweis** (national ID card), used when identity is unclear

**Address and contact**
- **Wo wohnen Sie?** / **Wie ist Ihre Anschrift?** (formal word for address)
- German order: Straße + Hausnummer, then Postleitzahl + Ort, for example "Hauptstraße 12, 10115 Berlin"
- **Unter welcher Telefonnummer sind Sie erreichbar?** (At what number can we reach you?)
- **Angehörige** (relatives) and the **Notfallkontakt** (emergency contact)

**Insurance**
- **gesetzliche Krankenversicherung (GKV)**: about 74 million people across roughly 95 Krankenkassen. Patients present the **elektronische Gesundheitskarte (eGK)**, which carries a lifelong **Versichertennummer** (one letter plus nine digits).
- **private Krankenversicherung (PKV)**: about 8.7 million people. They are invoiced directly.
- The eGK reverse side usually doubles as the **EHIC** (European Health Insurance Card) for travel within the EU.

**Grammar notes**
- **bei** takes the dative: "Ich bin **bei der** Techniker versichert", "**beim** (bei dem) Hausarzt".
- Use **Ihr/Ihre** (capitalised, formal "your"): Ihr Name, Ihre Adresse.
- Soften requests with **bitte** and **könnten Sie**: "Könnten Sie mir bitte Ihre Karte geben?"

**Safety**: confirm identity with two identifiers, usually full name plus **Geburtsdatum**, before any procedure or medication.
levels.phd:
The data-collection script reflects the structure of German healthcare law, so understanding the system explains the vocabulary.

**Statutory versus private.** Statutory insurance is governed by the **Sozialgesetzbuch V (SGB V)**. Employees below the **Versicherungspflichtgrenze** (compulsory insurance income threshold) must join a Krankenkasse. Higher earners, the self-employed and **Beamte** (civil servants) may opt for PKV. Beamte usually combine **Beihilfe** (state reimbursement of part of costs) with private cover. This is why asking "gesetzlich oder privat?" is not small talk: it changes billing. GKV services are billed via the **Kassenärztliche Vereinigung** using the **EBM** fee schedule; private care is billed to the patient under the **GOÄ** (Gebührenordnung für Ärzte). Patients who pay without insurance are **Selbstzahler**.

**The eGK as infrastructure.** The eGK is a smart card connected to the **Telematikinfrastruktur (TI)** run by **gematik**. At each quarter's first visit, the practice performs **Versichertenstammdatenmanagement (VSDM)**, an online check that the patient's master data and coverage are valid. The card stores the Versichertennummer, name, date of birth, address and insurer, and authenticates access to applications such as the **E-Rezept** (mandatory e-prescription since January 2024).

**ePA.** The **elektronische Patientenakte** moved to an **opt-out** model in 2025: every statutory patient receives one unless they file a **Widerspruch** (objection). Questions such as "Möchten Sie der ePA widersprechen?" may therefore appear in admission conversations.

**Special groups.** Asylum seekers in their first period are covered under the **Asylbewerberleistungsgesetz (AsylbLG)**, often with a paper **Behandlungsschein** or a regional card. EU visitors present the EHIC; others may need proof of travel insurance.

**Data protection.** Personal data are "special category" health data under the **DSGVO** (GDPR, Art. 9). Disclosure is limited by the **ärztliche Schweigepflicht**, which is criminally enforced by **§203 StGB**. Even confirming that someone is a patient can breach it without consent.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, the personal-data phase is about safety and rapport, and examiners in the **Fachsprachprüfung** listen for both.

**Identification errors.** Wrong-patient events are a recognised source of harm. Avoid closed confirmation questions ("Sind Sie Herr Müller?") because confused, hard-of-hearing or anxious patients often simply agree. Use open prompts: "Nennen Sie mir bitte Ihren vollen Namen und Ihr Geburtsdatum." Then compare with the **Patientenarmband** (wristband) and the chart. This is standard practice before transfusion, anaesthesia induction and the **Team-Time-Out** of the surgical safety checklist, where neurosurgical side and level checks depend on correct identity.

**Forms of address.** Use Herr/Frau + surname, and keep academic titles: "Frau Doktor Schulz". When gender or preferred form is unclear, ask "Wie darf ich Sie ansprechen?" Do not switch to du with adults unless invited. For children, du is normal, but parents get Sie.

**Phrasing that sounds native.**
- "Ich bräuchte noch ein paar Angaben zu Ihrer Person." (I still need a few details about you.)
- "Hat sich an Ihrer Adresse oder Krankenkasse etwas geändert?" (Has anything changed?)
- "Wer ist Ihr Ansprechpartner, falls etwas ist?" (Whom should we contact if needed?)
- Distinguish **Angehörige** from a legally empowered person: ask "Gibt es eine **Vorsorgevollmacht** oder einen **gesetzlichen Betreuer**?" This matters later for consent in patients who cannot decide for themselves.

**Pitfalls for learners.**
- **Krankenkasse** (statutory fund) is not the same as **Krankenversicherung** (insurance in general, including private).
- **Anschrift** is the formal written word; **Adresse** is fine in speech.
- "Ich bin bei der Barmer" uses dative feminine because Kasse names take die.
- Never disclose data to employers, police or relatives by phone without consent or a legal basis.

**Open issues.** ePA opt-out uptake, TI outages blocking VSDM, and identifying unconscious or unregistered patients (temporary IDs such as "Unbekannt, männlich") remain active operational problems in German hospitals.

keyPoints: Personalien = personal data: Vorname, Nachname, Geburtsdatum, Anschrift
Stay formal: Sie, Ihr/Ihre, Herr/Frau + surname
About 90% are gesetzlich versichert via a Krankenkasse; about 10% privat
Statutory patients present the elektronische Gesundheitskarte (eGK)
bei takes the dative: Ich bin bei der AOK versichert
Confirm identity with open questions: full name plus date of birth

test.q: What does 'Krankenkasse' mean?
test.explain: A Krankenkasse is a statutory health insurance fund such as the AOK or TK. It is not a payment desk.

test.q: Which is the polite way to ask an adult patient's name?
test.explain: Ihr (capitalised) is the formal 'your', used with Sie. The others use the informal du forms.

test.q: 'Gesetzlich versichert' means a patient is:
test.explain: Gesetzlich = statutory, through a Krankenkasse. Privat versichert is the private alternative.

test.q: Which card does a statutory patient show at reception?
test.explain: The elektronische Gesundheitskarte proves statutory insurance. The Personalausweis is a national ID card.

test.q: How many digits does a German Postleitzahl have?
test.explain: German postcodes have five digits, for example 10115 Berlin.

test.q: What does the Familienstand 'verwitwet' mean?
test.explain: Verwitwet = widowed. Geschieden is divorced, ledig is single, verheiratet is married.

test.q: What is the safest way to confirm a patient's identity before a procedure?
choices: Ask a yes/no question using the name
Ask for full name and date of birth
Check the room and bed number
Confirm the name with the nurse
test.explain: Two identifiers stated by the patient are the standard. Yes/no questions invite a confused patient to just agree.

test.q: Roughly what share of people in Germany are statutorily insured?
test.explain: About 90% (around 74 million) are in the GKV; about 10% are privately insured.

test.q: 'Wen sollen wir im Notfall benachrichtigen?' asks for:
test.explain: Benachrichtigen = notify. The question asks whom to contact in an emergency.

test.q: Ich bin ___ der AOK versichert.
test.explain: 'Versichert bei' + dative is the fixed phrase for being insured with a fund.

test.q: What is the German word for surname (the one beginning with N)?
test.explain: Nachname (also Familienname) is the surname; Vorname is the first name.

test.q: What is the German word for family doctor or GP?
test.explain: 'Wer ist Ihr Hausarzt?' asks who the patient's family doctor is.

kidTest.q: What does a Krankenkasse do?
kidTest.explain: It is like a shared piggy bank that pays for care when people are sick.

kidTest.q: What does 'Wie heißen Sie?' mean?
kidTest.explain: Heißen means to be called, so it asks your name.

kidTest.q: What does 'Wo wohnen Sie?' ask?
kidTest.explain: Wohnen means to live somewhere, so it asks your home.

kidTest.q: Why does the doctor's computer read the health card?
choices: To print a photo for the wall
To play a short welcome song
kidTest.explain: The card helps make sure the right person gets the right care.

kidTest.q: The health card is called a Gesundheits-k _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Gesundheitskarte means health card.

advancedTest.q: Why should you avoid 'Sind Sie Herr Müller?' when identifying a patient?
choices: Confused or anxious patients may agree even when wrong
German law forbids saying surnames before consent
It is grammatically incorrect in formal German speech
It uses du forms that sound rude to older adults
advancedTest.explain: Closed confirmation questions invite assent. An open request for name and birthdate exposes mismatches.

advancedTest.q: A patient says 'Ich bin privat versichert.' What follows for billing?
choices: The EHIC on the card back covers the whole visit
The practice reads the eGK and bills the Krankenkasse
The practice bills the patient directly under the GOÄ
The patient needs a Behandlungsschein under AsylbLG
advancedTest.explain: Private patients are invoiced directly under the GOÄ. eGK-based billing via the EBM applies to statutory patients.

advancedTest.q: Under the 2025 ePA model, a statutory patient who says nothing will most likely:
choices: Lose statutory cover until they register online
Have no record until signing a consent form
Need a private insurer to host the record
Receive an electronic record unless they object
advancedTest.explain: The ePA became opt-out: records are created by default and patients may file a Widerspruch.

advancedTest.q: A patient's employer phones asking whether the patient was admitted. What is the correct response?
choices: Give details since the employer pays insurance
Share data if the caller knows the birthdate
Decline, as even admission is confidential
Confirm admission but withhold the diagnosis
advancedTest.explain: Under the ärztliche Schweigepflicht (§203 StGB), even confirming someone is a patient needs consent or a legal basis.
